name: The Purāṇa as the fifth Veda

definitions.definition: Itihāsa and purāṇa are called the fifth Veda (BhP 1.4.20; cf. ChU 7.1.2); the Purāṇa was remembered by Brahmā before the Vedas (Matsya 53.3); it was composed out of compassion for those without access to the Veda (BhP 1.4.25); the Bhāgavata is the ripe fruit of the Veda-tree (1.1.3).

relations.note: the Purāṇa's eternal origin vs its human line of reciters

name: The five marks of a Purāṇa (pañcalakṣaṇa)

definitions.definition: A Purāṇa treats creation (sarga), secondary creation (pratisarga), dynasties (vaṃśa), the Manu-intervals (manvantara) and the deeds of the dynasties (vaṃśānucarita) (VP 3.6.24; KūP 1.1.12; Matsya 53.65); the Bhāgavata calls the five-mark Purāṇas the 'small' ones (12.7.10).

name: The Bhāgavata's ten marks (daśalakṣaṇa)

definitions.definition: Two lists: (1) BhP 2.10.1 - sarga, visarga, sthāna, poṣaṇa, ūti, manvantara, īśānukathā, nirodha, mukti, āśraya, the first nine told for understanding the tenth; (2) BhP 12.7.9 - sarga, visarga, vṛtti, rakṣā, antara (manvantara), vaṃśa, vaṃśānucarita, saṃsthā, hetu, apāśraya.

members: list 2.10.1: sarga, visarga, sthāna, poṣaṇa, ūti, manvantara, īśānukathā, nirodha, mukti, āśraya
list 12.7.9: sarga, visarga, vṛtti, rakṣā, antara, vaṃśa, vaṃśānucarita, saṃsthā, hetu, apāśraya

relations.note: ten marks of the 'great' vs five of the 'small' Purāṇas (BhP 12.7.10)

definitions.definition: The lists agree on eighteen but differ: VP 3.6.21-23 and BhP 12.7.23-24 name the Śiva (Śaiva); Matsya 53 and the Nārada's index name the Vāyu; KūP 1.1.13-15 names both, taking the 'Vāyavīya' as the Brahmāṇḍa. Traditional extents total four lakh verses (BhP 12.13.4-9).

Secondary Purāṇas told by sages or by Vyāsa's disciples (VP 3.6.23; KūP 1.11.280); the Kūrma lists eighteen (Sanatkumāra, Nārasiṃha, Skānda, Śivadharma, Āścarya, Nāradīya, Kāpila, Mānava, Auśanasa, Brahmāṇḍa, Vāruṇa, Kālikā, Māheśvara, Sāmba, Saura, Pārāśara, Mārīca, Bhārgava); the Matsya adds that every Purāṇa apart from the eighteen issued from them (53.64).

name: The classification of Purāṇas by the guṇas

definitions.definition: Matsya 53.68-69: sāttvika Purāṇas glorify Hari, rājasa Brahmā, tāmasa Agni and Śiva, mixed ones Sarasvatī and the ancestors. The Padma (as cited) assigns six Purāṇas to each guṇa; the Garuḍa's Brahmakāṇḍa gives a different, graded list. Śaiva texts counter with lists in which most Purāṇas glorify Śiva (not checked here).

name: The transmission of the Purāṇa

definitions.definition: Brahmā remembered the one Purāṇa first; Vyāsa condenses it in each Dvāpara; he gave the Purāṇa-saṃhitā to Romaharṣaṇa, whose disciples made saṃhitās, giving four root saṃhitās (VP 3.6.15-19; BhP 12.7.5-7 with a different list of six disciples); the Sūta Ugraśravas recites to Śaunaka at Naimiṣa; each Purāṇa also has its own chain of speakers (e.g. Viṣṇu - Garuḍa; Parāśara - Maitreya; Śuka - Parīkṣit).

members: VP: Sumati, Agnivarcas, Mitrāyu, Śāṃśapāyana, Akṛtavraṇa (Kāśyapa), Sāvarṇi
BhP: Trayyāruṇi, Kaśyapa, Sāvarṇi, Akṛtavraṇa, Vaiśampāyana, Hārīta

definitions.definition: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 divine years plus junctions (4,800, 3,600, 2,400, 1,200), dharma declining through them; the means of each age differ (meditation, sacrifice, worship, singing the name).

name: Kalpa, the day of Brahmā and his lifetime

definitions.definition: A thousand cycles of four ages (mahāyugas) with fourteen Manus make a day of Brahmā (kalpa), followed by a night of equal length; Brahmā lives a hundred years of such days, in two halves (parārdha); the present is the first day of his second half (Śveta-Vārāha kalpa, seventh manvantara, Kali age - tradition's reckoning).

name: The manvantaras and the fourteen Manus

definitions.definition: Each day of Brahmā has fourteen Manus: Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Uttama (Auttama), Tāmasa, Raivata, Cākṣuṣa, Vaivasvata (the present), then the Sāvarṇis beginning with Sūrya-Sāvarṇi (the Devī Māhātmya's Suratha); each interval has its Indra, gods, seven sages and avatāra; names of the later Manus vary between Purāṇas.

notes: MkP 50-100 (chapter colophons checked) narrates the manvantaras.

definitions.definition: Constant (nitya) - the continual perishing of beings; occasional (naimittika) - of the three worlds at the end of Brahmā's day; elemental (prākṛtika) - of the whole egg into Prakṛti at the end of his life; final (ātyantika) - liberation by knowledge.

Primary creation (sarga) is the emergence of mahat, the elements and senses from the unmanifest; secondary creation (visarga/pratisarga) is Brahmā's fashioning of the worlds and beings - Brahmā born on the lotus from the navel of the Lord lying on the waters.

name: The nine creations of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa

definitions.definition: Three primary (of mahat, the elements, the senses), five secondary (immobile, animals, gods, humans, anugraha) and the Kaumāra creation of the Kumāras, both primary and secondary.
Pradhāna, puruṣa, the manifest (vyakta) and time (kāla) are forms of the one Viṣṇu, the supreme Brahman.

Seven upper worlds - Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svar, Mahar, Janas, Tapas, Satya - and seven lower worlds (the pātālas) within the cosmic egg; the first three (trailokya) are dissolved every night of Brahmā; the yogin rises through them (BhP 2.2.22-31).
BhP 5.24.7: Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala, Mahātala, Rasātala, Pātāla; VP 2.5.2: Atala, Vitala, Nitala, Gabhastimat, Mahākhya, Sutala, Pātāla - realms of daityas and nāgas, full of delights.

name: Bhū-maṇḍala: Meru, seven island-continents and seven oceans

definitions.definition: The earth-disc: Jambudvīpa with Meru at its centre, surrounded by the salt ocean; then Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka and Puṣkara dvīpas, each ringed by an ocean (of sugar-cane juice, wine, ghee, curd, milk and sweet water respectively), then a golden land, the Lokāloka range and darkness; Jambudvīpa has nine varṣas, of which Bhārata is the land of action.

notes: Order of the oceans from memory (VP 2.2-4; BhP 5.16-20); Phase D to check.

name: Bhārata as the land of action

definitions.definition: Only in Bhārata are deeds done that bear fruit and lead to heaven or liberation; the gods envy those born there (VP 2.3.22-25).

Places of torment below the earth in the south within the three worlds, ruled by Yama, each matched to classes of sin (BhP 5.26: twenty-eight; VP 2.6 and MkP 12 other lists); release comes by exhaustion of the karma, by remembrance of the Lord, or by the transfer of a righteous person's merit (MkP 15); VP 2.6.46 teaches that heaven and hell are names for merit and sin.

Yama (Dharmarāja), king of the ancestors, judges the dead by their deeds under the Lord's command; the sinful see him terrible, the virtuous gentle; he has no power over the Lord's devotees; the Ekādaśī vow can empty his realm.

The dead, bound by Yama's messengers in a body for suffering, is dragged south over thorns, stones and burning ground to Yama's city: in MkP in twelve days, in the Garuḍa over a year past sixteen cities where he eats the monthly piṇḍas, crossing the Vaitaraṇī; in the Bhāgavata in two or three muhūrtas. Gifts made in life (umbrellas, sandals, food, the Vaitaraṇī cow) ease the road.

At the appointed time illness arises, senses and strength fail, the heat of the body stirred by wind breaks the vital points, udāna rises, speech fails and sight whirls, Yama's messengers are seen; the thumb-sized person leaves the body (through an upper or lower opening according to destiny), looking back at home; the good die easily, the wicked in terror.

Immediately after death the being takes an airy conveyance-body (ātivāhika); over the first ten days the piṇḍas offered by the sons build, limb by limb, a hand-sized body for the preta, which joins the airy body; the preta feels hunger from the tenth day.

The condition of the dead between death and union with the ancestors; it becomes fixed for those who die badly, do great wrong or lack the rites (e.g. no bull released on the eleventh day), who then suffer hunger and thirst and trouble their kin (dreams, signs); it is ended by śrāddha, gifts, nārāyaṇa-bali and hearing sacred texts (the Bhāgavata saptāha frees Dhundhukārī).
By sapiṇḍīkaraṇa the preta is joined to the three generations of ancestors and thereafter receives the pārvaṇa and annual śrāddhas; offerings at Gayā free the ancestors.

name: The cycle of rites for the dead

definitions.definition: Cremation; ten days of piṇḍa and water (building the preta-body); the eleventh-day rites (vṛṣotsarga, the 'middle sixteen'); sapiṇḍīkaraṇa on the twelfth day or later; monthly śrāddhas through the first year (feeding the traveller on Yama's road); the annual śrāddha; periods of impurity for the kin.

What one remembers at death shapes what follows: Bharata dying absorbed in a fawn became a deer; Ajāmila calling 'Nārāyaṇa' was rescued; remembrance of Nārāyaṇa at the end is the highest gain of life (BhP 2.1.6); the dying should meditate on the Lord (12.3.50); the yogin whose karma remains should recall yoga at departure (MkP 42.16-17); Kāśī tradition speaks of Śiva's instruction at death.

relations.note: absorption at death vs absorption through a lifelong emotion

definitions.definition: The yogin may leave the body at will through the crown (BhP 2.2.15-21) and either be liberated at once or rise by the suṣumnā through Agni, Śiśumāra, Mahar- and Satyaloka and be liberated with Brahmā at the dissolution (2.2.22-31); the Vāyavīya also speaks of departure at will (ŚiP 7.2.37.26).

Portents by which the yogin knows his death: not seeing Arundhatī, the pole-star, the moon's shadow or the Milky Way (death within a year), a rayless sun, certain dreams, loss of shadow and bodily changes (shorter spans).

The perfected one does not notice whether the body stands or sits, as a drunk his cloth; the body lives on until its karma is spent, but he does not re-enter the dream (BhP 3.28.37-38); Keśidhvaja acts without attachment and is freed.
The one non-dual reality called Brahman, Paramātman and Bhagavān (BhP 1.2.11); Bhagavān possesses the six excellences and is properly Vāsudeva (VP 6.5.74-79); Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself (BhP 1.3.28).

relations.note: the one Lord seen by function

definitions.definition: The Lord (or his Puruṣa form) descends age after age in innumerable forms to protect the world; all are portions and parts except Kṛṣṇa, Bhagavān himself (BhP 1.3); in the Śaiva and Śākta Purāṇas Śiva and the Goddess likewise appear repeatedly ('whenever trouble arises I will descend', DM 11).

name: The lists of avatāras

definitions.definition: BhP 1.3 lists twenty-two by ordinal; BhP 2.7 adds others (Hayagrīva, Haṃsa, Hari who saved Gajendra, the Manvantara-avatāras); the Agni (2-16, 49) and Garuḍa (1.142) teach ten (Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa or Balarāma, Buddha, Kalki); a count of twenty-four is common in later tradition (its membership varies and no single Bhāgavata verse gives it).

members: ten: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa/Balarāma, Buddha, Kalki

twenty-two (BhP 1.3): Kumāras, Varāha, Nārada, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Kapila, Dattātreya, Yajña, Ṛṣabha, Pṛthu, Matsya, Kūrma, Dhanvantari, Mohinī, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Vyāsa, Rāma, Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki

definitions.definition: One Lord takes the names Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva for creation, maintenance and destruction (VP 1.2.66); in the Devī Māhātmya and Devī Bhāgavata the three receive their bodies and powers from the Goddess.

name: The identity of Hari and Hara

definitions.definition: Passages that make Viṣṇu and Śiva one: the Kūrma's Īśvara Gītā, Hari as all the gods in Gajendra's rescue, Śambhu as the foremost Vaiṣṇava (BhP 12.13.16); set against sectarian passages that subordinate one to the other.

relations.note: unity vs Śiva's superiority to Brahmā and Viṣṇu

name: Śiva as niṣkala and sakala; the liṅga

definitions.definition: Śiva alone is both partless Brahman and with form, so he alone is worshipped both in the formless liṅga and in the image; the unmarked (aliṅga) Śiva is the root of the mark (liṅga).

name: The appearance of the liṅga of fire

definitions.definition: While Brahmā and Viṣṇu disputed supremacy a boundless column of fire appeared; neither could find its ends; Śiva appeared from it.

name: The Goddess as Mahāmāyā and the supreme

definitions.definition: The Goddess is eternal, the world is her form; she deludes even the wise and, pleased, liberates; she is the cause of all worlds, the primordial Prakṛti beyond Hari and Hara; all knowledges and women are her forms; she alone exists and her powers return into her.

name: The three episodes of the Devī Māhātmya

definitions.definition: First carita (ch. 1): Yoganidrā leaves Viṣṇu to slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha; middle carita (chs. 2-4): the Goddess from the gods' radiance slays Mahiṣa; last carita (chs. 5-13): Ambikā with Kālī-Cāmuṇḍā and the Mothers slays Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa-Muṇḍa, Raktabīja, Niśumbha and Śumbha.

In the recitation tradition the presiding deities of the three caritas are Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī, derived from the primordial Mahālakṣmī (Prādhānika Rahasya); the thirteen chapters themselves do not use these three names for the caritas.

relations.note: later ancillary texts map the three forms onto the three episodes

definitions.definition: Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī and Aindrī - the gods' śaktis who fight with the Goddess and then dissolve into her.
The Goddess's supreme abode - the jewel island with enclosures of metals and gems and the Cintāmaṇi palace (Devī Bhāgavata), and Lalitā's city Śrīnagara with its enclosures (Lalitopākhyāna).
Bhaṇḍāsura, born from the ashes of Kāma burnt by Śiva, conquers the worlds; Lalitā arises from the gods' sacrificial fire, weds Kāmeśvara, defeats Bhaṇḍa with her śaktis and revives Kāma.
Parā (Viṣṇu-śakti), aparā (kṣetrajña) and avidyā-karma, which veils the kṣetrajña and causes saṃsāra; the world as the śakti of Brahman like the light of a fire.

name: Māyāmoha: the Purāṇic account of Buddhist and Jain teaching

definitions.definition: The Purāṇas report that Viṣṇu emitted a deluding form (Māyāmoha), or became the Buddha, to lead the demons away from the Veda by teaching Jain and Buddhist doctrine (VP 3.17-18; Agni 16; BhP 1.3.24; cf. BhP 5.6.9 on the Arhat king) - an opponent's report.

The highest dharma is that which produces unmotivated, uninterrupted devotion to the Lord (BhP 1.2.6); devotion beginning with the name is the supreme dharma known to the mahājanas (6.3.22); neither yoga nor Sāṃkhya wins the Lord as devotion does (11.14.20).

Hearing, singing, remembering, serving the feet, worship, obeisance, servitude, friendship and self-offering (BhP 7.5.23-24); the Śiva Purāṇa's three means (hearing, singing, reflection) are a Śaiva counterpart.
Tāmasa (with violence, pride, anger in view), rājasa (for objects, fame, power), sāttvika (to remove karma, as duty) and nirguṇa devotion that flows unbroken to the Lord (BhP 3.29.7-12).

name: The five liberations and their refusal

definitions.definition: Sālokya, sārṣṭi, sāmīpya, sārūpya and sāyujya/ekatva; pure devotees do not accept them without service (BhP 3.29.13) and desire neither powers nor freedom from rebirth (11.14.14).

name: The power of the divine name

definitions.definition: Uttering the Lord's name, even indirectly, destroys all sin and is the best expiation (BhP 6.2.9-14); it is the fearless way for all (2.1.11), the supreme dharma (6.3.22) and the means of the Kali age (12.3.51-52; VP 6.2.17); offences against it hinder its fruit (Padma, as cited).

name: Absorption through any emotion fixed on the Lord

definitions.definition: Desire, anger, fear, affection, oneness or friendship constantly directed at Hari bring absorption in him: the gopīs by desire, Kaṃsa by fear, Śiśupāla by hatred (BhP 7.1.30; 10.29.15; VP 4.15.2).
The gopīs' longing when Kṛṣṇa vanishes or departs, which Kṛṣṇa says he causes so that their minds dwell on him; Uddhava wishes to be the dust of their feet.
Kṛṣṇa's dance with the gopīs (BhP 10.29-33), whose hearing gives supreme devotion and removes lust; not to be imitated by those who are not lords (10.33.30-31).
Gajendra surrendering to the nameless supreme; the gods taking refuge in the Goddess, 'intent on saving those who come for refuge'.

name: The dharma of the Kali age

definitions.definition: Kali is full of faults, and gambling, drink, illicit women, slaughter and gold are its dwellings; yet in Kali merit comes quickly: singing the name gives what earlier ages won by meditation, sacrifice and worship, and śūdras and women gain merit easily by service.

name: The means proper to each age

definitions.definition: Meditation in Kṛta, sacrifice in Tretā, worship in Dvāpara, singing the name in Kali (BhP 12.3.52; VP 6.2.17).

The Purāṇas teach the eight limbs with their own contents: the ethical lists vary (MkP 41.16-17; ŚiP 7.2.37.18-19), the support of dhāraṇā and dhyāna is the deity's form (VP 6.7; BhP 3.28, 11.14) or Śiva (ŚiP 7.2.39), and the goal is joining the mind with Brahman (VP 6.7.31) or nirvāṇa, Maheśa's state (LiP 1.8.5).

name: The auspicious support of the mind (śubhāśraya)

definitions.definition: The mind in yoga needs a support: Brahman in its formed and formless aspects; since the beginner cannot hold the formless, he meditates on Viṣṇu's form, the ground of all powers, which alone purifies (VP 6.7.45-78).
Beings' contemplation is of Brahman (the Sanandanas), of action (gods down to plants), or of both (Hiraṇyagarbha and others with office).

Eight principal powers of the Lord (aṇimā, mahimā, laghimā, prāpti, prākāmya, īśitā, vaśitā, kāmāvasāyitā), ten from the guṇas and five lesser ones, each gained by a dhāraṇā on the Lord - and all obstacles for one seeking him.

relations.note: the powers waste the time of one seeking the Lord

name: The first signs of progress in yoga

definitions.definition: Lightness/freedom from greed, health, gentleness, pleasant smell, scant excreta, radiance, clarity, a pleasant voice; others praise the yogin, creatures do not fear him, he is untroubled by heat and cold (MkP 39.63-65).

Viṣṇu is worshipped through the conduct of one's varṇa and āśrama (VP 3.8.9); the Purāṇas add vows, pilgrimage, gifts, śrāddha, image worship and temple building as dharma for all classes, and praise devotion above all rites.

A self-imposed observance for a day or period (fast, vigil, worship, gifts), bound to a lunar date and deity, with a story and a promised fruit; Ekādaśī, Śivarātri, Navarātra and the Kātyāyanī vow are examples.

name: Pilgrimage places and their inner meaning

definitions.definition: Earthly tīrthas are holy by the power of earth and water and the presence of sages; seven cities give liberation; but the virtues are inner tīrthas, purity of mind the highest, and devotees themselves make tīrthas holy.

Giving to worthy recipients at due times and places; the sixteen great gifts (tulāpuruṣa, hiraṇyagarbha, etc.); gifts made in life or at death ease the road of the dead (Vaitaraṇī cow, umbrellas, sandals, food).
